[PMID 42902416 | PMC13685282 full text via pmc_xml] Cardiac magnetic resonance with myocardial strain as a predictor of anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity in patients with lymphoma: a prospective multimodality study. :: Anthracyclines remain a cornerstone of curative chemotherapy regimens for lymphoma, but cardiovascular complications related to their use are common and serious adverse events that can compromise both oncologic outcomes and long-term survival [1]. A clearer understanding of the mechanisms underlying cancer therapy–related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) is essential for early detection and appropriate management of cardiovascular complications, particularly in high-risk patients [1].
Asymptomatic CTRCD is frequent during anthracycline chemotherapy and is most often detected by transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), including myocardial deformation analysis by speckle-tracking strain, and by serial measurement of cardiac biomarkers such as high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT) and NT-proBNP [2]. Despite its limitations—including inter-observer variability and load dependence—a LVEF decline greater than 10% points to less than 50% assessed by TTE remains the most widely accepted definition of CTRCD [2]. Early diagnosis of CTRCD is essential to prevent symptomatic heart failure and death, and may also avoid chemotherapy interruption or dose reduction, both of which are independently associated with worse oncologic outcomes [3].
Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is the gold standard non-invasive method to evaluate biventricular volumes and ejection fraction and has assumed a growing role in cardio-oncology [4, 5]. Beyond volumetric assessment, CMR enables tissue characterization through native T1 mapping and extracellular volume (ECV) quantification, which have been proposed as non-invasive markers of diffuse interstitial fibrosis associated with anthracycline exposure [6, 7]. Histopathological studies have demonstrated that anthracycline cardiotoxicity is characterized by a diffuse pattern of myocardial fibrosis, supporting the rationale for tissue mapping techniques in this setting [8, 9]. In parallel, CMR provides multiple approaches for the quantification of myocardial deformation, including feature tracking, tissue tagging, and strain encoding [10–12], which have shown prognostic and diagnostic value across a wide range of cardiovascular conditions [13–15]. Data on the combined use of these techniques in patients undergoing anthracycline-based chemotherapy for lymphoma, however, remain limited.
In this prospective study, we investigated whether multiparametric CMR—incorporating T1 mapping, ECV, and feature-tracking myocardial strain—is useful for the early detection of CTRCD in patients with lymphoma treated with anthracyclines, and how its performance compares with conventional TTE and circulating cardiac biomarkers.
Study design and population. This was a single-center, prospective, observational cohort study conducted at the Instituto do Cancer do Estado de Sao Paulo (ICESP) and Instituto do Coracao (InCor), Hospital das Clinicas HCFMUSP, Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Sao Paulo, Brazil, from June 2017 to January 2020. The study protocol was approved by the Scientific Committee (NP 819/15 and NP 1132/17) and by the Research Ethics Committee of ICESP, and conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided written informed consent prior to enrollment.
Eligible participants were adults (≥ 18 years) with a clinical and histopathological diagnosis of lymphoma scheduled to receive first-line anthracycline-based chemotherapy. Exclusion criteria included previous heart disease of any etiology; systolic blood pressure > 180 mmHg; renal dysfunction with plasma creatinine > 2.0 mg/dL; pregnancy or breastfeeding; HIV infection treated with antiretroviral therapy; the need for emergency chemotherapy; impaired performance status (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group ≥ 3 and/or Karnofsky Performance Status scale ≤ 60); life expectancy < 1 year; and any contraindications to CMR.
Chemotherapy regimens. Standardized first-line curative regimens were prescribed according to current institutional protocols and international guidelines. Patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma received R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone) or R-EPOCH (rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin), while patients with Hodgkin lymphoma received ABVD (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine). The cumulative doxorubicin dose ranged from 200 to 400 mg/m². Detailed chemotherapy schedules are provided in Supplemental Table 1.
Cardiovascular evaluation and definition of CTRCD. All patients underwent evaluation at baseline (visit 0), prior to chemotherapy, with information about clinical history, cardiovascular risk factors, use of medications, and a complete physical examination. Subsequent visits were scheduled at visit 1 (after the third chemotherapy cycle), visit 2 (at chemotherapy completion), and visit 3 (12 months after chemotherapy initiation) (see Additional file 1). Additional consultations were performed as clinically indicated. Patients diagnosed with CTRCD were followed and treated according to current guideline recommendations [2]. CTRCD was initially defined as a reduction in LVEF ≥ 5% to < 55% with symptoms of heart failure, or an asymptomatic reduction in LVEF ≥ 10% to < 55% [16].
In addition, CTRCD was classified according to the 2022 ESC Cardio-Oncology Guidelines into three categories: (a) mild, defined as preserved LVEF (≥ 50%) with a new relative decline in GLS > 15% from baseline and/or a new rise in cardiac biomarkers; [2] moderate, defined as either a ≥ 10% point reduction in LVEF to 40–49%, or a < 10-point reduction in LVEF to 40–49% accompanied by a new relative decline in GLS > 15% and/or a new elevation in cardiac biomarkers; and (c) severe, defined as a new LVEF reduction to < 40% [17].
Cardiac biomarkers. NT–pro brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT) were measured at visits 0, 1, and 2. Detailed assay methodology is provided in the Supplemental Methods.
Transthoracic echocardiography. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) was performed using a GE Vivid E9 ultrasound system. Two experienced physicians performed the studies, and each patient was followed by the same operator throughout the study to minimize inter-observer variability. Studies were obtained at visits 0, 1, 2, and 3. Image acquisition followed standard parasternal and apical views with morphological and functional assessment, using two-dimensional imaging and Doppler-derived flow data [18, 19]. Diastolic function and right ventricular parameters were systematically assessed. The left ventricular mass index was calculated according to current recommendations. The details of analysis are provided in the Additional file 1.
For two-dimensional speckle-tracking analysis, the echocardiographic device was set to record three consecutive cardiac cycles with a 100 ms buffer before and after each cycle. Second-harmonic gray-scale imaging was used, with frame rates between 50 and 80 frames/s, as recommended by the manufacturer and by current literature.
The systolic event window was defined by aortic valve opening and closure. Apical 3-, 4-, and 2-chamber views were acquired and stored digitally for offline analysis.
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. All patients underwent CMR on a General Electric 3.0 T CV/i scanner (Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA). CMR was performed at visit 0, visit 1, and visit 2. The full scan protocol and acquisition parameters are detailed in the Supplemental Methods. The protocol consisted of retrospectively ECG-gated steady-state free precession cine imaging; pre- and post-contrast T1 mapping; dark-blood triple inversion-recovery fast spin-echo imaging; and two-dimensional phase-sensitive late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging.
Late gadolinium enhancement images were acquired 10 to 15 min after intravenous gadolinium injection (ProHance®, gadoteridol 279.3 mg/mL) at a dose of 0.2 mmol/kg, in all standard long-axis and short-axis views. Visual and quantitative analyses were performed using the CVI 42 software package (Release version 5.5.1 [559]; Circle Cardiovascular Imaging Inc., Calgary, Canada).
T1 mapping sequences were acquired before (native T1) and 15 min after contrast injection using a Modified Look-Locker Inversion Recovery sequence (sampling pattern 3 [3]3 [3]5) in the diastolic phase at three standard short-axis slices (basal, mid-ventricular, and apical). Native T1 times and ECV were calculated by two trained observers using CVI 42, with ECV derived from same-day pre-contrast hematocrit. The entire myocardium was included, excluding only areas with visual artifacts. Motion correction was applied. Ten healthy control volunteers underwent non-contrast CMR with the identical protocol to assess normal native T1 values (see Additional file 1).
Feature-tracking strain analysis was performed with the Tissue Tracking module of CVI 42 to derive global longitudinal (GLS-CMR), circumferential (GCS-CMR), and radial (GRS-CMR) strain. Endocardial and epicardial contours and the interventricular insertion points were manually delineated on the short-axis stack and on the 2-, 3-, and 4-chamber long-axis views. All analyses were performed by a single observer and reviewed by a senior observer blinded to clinical data.
Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test, likelihood ratio test, or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. Continuous variables with normal distribution are presented as mean ± standard deviation, and non-normal variables as median (interquartile range, 1st to 3rd quartile). Normality was assessed by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. The longitudinal evolution of laboratory, echocardiographic, and CMR parameters was assessed using linear and logistic mixed-effects models, depending on whether the outcome was continuous or dichotomous. The patient was modeled as a random effect to account for repeated measurements. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used for paired comparisons between visits. Comparisons of CTRCD distributions assessed by TTE and CMR were performed using McNemar’s test, and inter-modality agreement was quantified using Cohen’s kappa coefficient. Between-group comparisons of CMR parameters in patients with and without CTRCD were performed using the mixed linear model. Reproducibility analysis was performed to assess random fluctuations in repeated measurements obtained from the same group on different occasions. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was used to quantify the overall agreement between two measurements obtained from the same patient. ICC values approaching 1 indicate excellent agreement and high reproducibility between measurements. To facilitate visualization of the agreement between the two measurements, Bland–Altman plots were also generated.
Sample size was estimated using G*Power 3 for macOS. Assuming an effect size defined by a mean difference of 2% in LVEF, a standard deviation of 4.1% (based on the placebo arm of a previous study [20], an alpha error of 0.05, and a power of 0.80, a minimum of 47 participants was required to detect significant changes in repeated measures; the final sample was modestly oversized to compensate for potential dropouts. Two-sided p-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 20 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) and Stata Statistical Software, Release 18 (StataCorp, College Station, TX).
Of 161 lymphoma patients screened for eligibility, 111 were excluded based on eligibility criteria and one was excluded due to inadequate echocardiographic image quality (Supplemental Fig. 2). TTE demonstrated a significant decline in LVEF by the Simpson method (from 62.92 ± 5.61% at baseline to 60.23 ± 5.41% at Visit 2; p = 0.037) and progressive worsening of GLS (from − 19.84 ± 2.35% to − 18.31 ± 2.73%; p = 0.001), consistent with early impairment of myocardial contractility.
CMR confirmed and extended these findings, demonstrating a significant reduction in LVEF (from 61.98 ± 6.08% to 57.34 ± 7.29%; p < 0.001) and a progressive deterioration in myocardial deformation indices, including GLS, GCS, and GRS (p < 0.001 for all) (Fig. 2). There was also a significant increase in end-systolic volume index (ESVi) and a reduction in left ventricular mass indexed to body surface area, suggesting early adverse remodeling related to cardiotoxicity. Right ventricular ejection fraction also decreased significantly during follow-up (54.14 ± 8.34% to 52.69 ± 8.88%; p = 0.030).

Bland–Altman analysis demonstrated good agreement between echocardiography- and CMR-derived LVEF measurements across all study visits (Fig. 4). At baseline (Visit 0), the mean bias was 0.97%, with 95% limits of agreement ranging from − 9.44% to 11.39%. At Visit 1, the mean bias increased slightly to 2.24% (95% limits of agreement: −9.39% to 14.38%), and at Visit 2, the mean bias was 2.89% (95% limits of agreement: −8.31% to 14.10%).

Overall, the small mean differences indicate good concordance between modalities for LVEF assessment. Most measurements were distributed evenly around the mean bias, with no clear evidence of proportional bias across the range of LVEF values. Although a slight tendency for higher LVEF values by echocardiography compared with CMR was observed at follow-up visits, the overall agreement remained acceptable throughout the study period.
According to the criterion of LVEF reduction ≥ 5% to < 55% with heart failure symptoms or an asymptomatic reduction ≥ 10% to < 55%, CTRCD was identified in 7 patients (14.9%) by CMR and 5 (10.6%) by TTE (see Additional file 1). The difference between modalities was not statistically significant (p = 0.625), and agreement at any visit was substantial (Cohen’s κ = 0.619; p < 0.001).
Figure 5 shows the agreement between echocardiography and CMR for CTRCD classification. Overall concordance was observed in 43 of 47 patients (91.5%), including 39 patients without CTRCD and 4 patients with CTRCD identified by both modalities. Discordant classifications occurred in four patients: three were classified as having CTRCD only by CMR, whereas one was classified as having CTRCD only by echocardiography. Two patients (4.3%) met criteria for moderate or severe cardiotoxicity (≥ 10% point reduction in LVEF to < 50%).

Table 4 shows the longitudinal CMR findings according to CTRCD status, with comparisons of group effects, time effectsm and group-by-time interactions derived from mixed-effects model. For CMR-derived LVEF, a significant interaction effect was observed (p = 0.001). While no between-group differences were present at baseline, patients without CTRCD exhibited higher LVEF values during follow-up. Within-group analyses showed that LVEF remained relatively preserved in the non-CTRCD group, whereas patients with CTRCD demonstrated a significant decline from baseline. No significant interaction, time, or group effects were observed for RVEF. Global native T1 values showed a significant group-by-time interaction (p = 0.010). No temporal changes were observed in the non-CTRCD group, whereas patients with CTRCD exhibited higher T1 values during follow-up compared with baseline. Additionally, baseline T1 values were lower in the CTRCD group, with no differences between groups at later visits. In contrast, ECV remained stable over time and did not differ between groups. Regarding myocardial deformation parameters, GLS demonstrated a significant time effect (p < 0.001), with lower values during follow-up in both groups, but without significant interaction. GCS showed a significant interaction effect (p = 0.036); although values were similar at baseline, patients without CTRCD had higher GCS values at follow-up. Finally, GRS demonstrated significant time (p < 0.001) and group effects (p = 0.047), with lower values at follow-up in both groups and overall lower values among patients with CTRCD.

In this prospective cohort of patients with lymphoma undergoing anthracycline-based chemotherapy, we observed early and progressive subclinical cardiac changes detected by both TTE and CMR. The consistent decline in LVEF and the deterioration of GLS by both modalities indicate early myocardial dysfunction in the absence of overt clinical symptoms, and the parallel rise in hs-cTnT supports the occurrence of subclinical myocardial injury during treatment. NT-proBNP did not change significantly, possibly reflecting transient hemodynamic fluctuations rather than sustained ventricular overload. Additionally, patients with CTRCD exhibited higher native T1 values on CMR during follow-up, a finding that may reflect early myocardial tissue alterations associated with cardiotoxicity. Taken together, these findings support the utility of a multiparametric imaging strategy—integrating CMR, echocardiography, and biomarkers—for the early detection of cardiotoxicity, with the potential to enable timely intervention and prevent irreversible damage even in low-risk patients exposed to high cumulative doses of anthracyclines.
Cardiac dysfunction induced by anthracyclines remains a clinical challenge in cardio-oncology. In the present cohort, 39.6% of patients exhibited elevated troponin T levels (> 0.013 ng/mL), consistent with subclinical myocardial injury. This aligns with previous studies reporting troponin elevations in 30–50% of patients undergoing anthracycline-based chemotherapy, even in the absence of overt functional decline [21, 22]. hs-cTnT levels showed a marked and progressive increase over the follow-up period, rising significantly from baseline to visit 2, a pattern consistent with cumulative myocardial injury related to treatment exposure.
In our cohort, CTRCD was identified in 10.6% of patients by TTE and 14.9% by CMR, with no statistically significant difference between imaging modalities. These observations are in keeping with the findings of Nazir et al., who reported a mean bias of − 3.7% (± 7.6%) between 2D echocardiography and CMR for LVEF, and approximately 10% misclassification at the clinically relevant 50% LVEF threshold [23]. These convergent findings illustrate the trade-off between diagnostic sensitivity and clinical practicality: while CMR may offer superior sensitivity for diagnostic of CTRCD, TTE remains a valuable, widely available tool for routine cardiotoxicity surveillance.
Advanced imaging modalities revealed more sensitive markers of myocardial dysfunction. Echocardiographic GLS reductions exceeding 15% from baseline were observed in 15.2% of patients at visit 1, increasing to 21.4% at the 12-month follow-up. CMR-derived GLS reductions were even more pronounced, reaching 34.1% at visit 1 and 43.9% at visit 2. These findings are consistent with the 2022 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Cardio-Oncology Guidelines, which recommend myocardial strain imaging and biomarkers for the early detection of CTRCD [24].
Our results are corroborated by the study of Voß et al., which demonstrated that anthracycline therapy induces a decline in myocardial contractility in virtually all exposed patients, regardless of baseline cardiovascular risk. In their cohort of 59 low-risk breast cancer patients, all experienced a measurable drop in CMR-assessed LVEF immediately post-therapy, and more than half developed CTRCD within 12 months, defined by reductions in LVEF, GLS, and/or elevated cardiac biomarkers [25]. These findings emphasize the pervasive nature of anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity and the necessity for vigilant cardiac monitoring.
Our findings are consistent with previous observations demonstrating that quantitative CMR tissue characterization parameters show only modest changes during chemotherapy and may be influenced by temporal and observer variability [26]. In our cohort, patients who developed CTRCD exhibited increased native T1 values over time, whereas ECV remained unchanged. This pattern likely reflects the early stage of anthracycline-related myocardial injury, characterized by edema and subtle myocardial tissue alterations rather than established diffuse fibrosis. Because native T1 is sensitive to both intracellular and extracellular changes, it may detect myocardial damage earlier in the disease process, while ECV abnormalities are more likely to emerge later, when extracellular matrix expansion and diffuse fibrosis become more prominent. Therefore, the observed increase in native T1, particularly among patients exposed to higher cumulative anthracycline doses, supports its potential role as an early marker of cardiotoxic myocardial injury.
This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. The study was conducted at a single center with a relatively small sample; however, the number of patients evaluated is similar to that of most prospective studies that have evaluated CMR-based detection of cardiotoxicity. The study was nonrandomized and lacked a control group. The follow-up with CMR was short; however, the purpose of this study was the early identification of CTRCD, and a long-term follow-up will be reported in the future (28). Finally, lack of adjustment for potential confounders such as age, cardiovascular risk factors, sex, and cumulative anthracycline dose limits causal inference from the imaging findings due to the reduced sample size. The present study did not systematically evaluate the initiation of cardioprotective therapies, as treatment decisions were left to the discretion of the local treating physicians. Data regarding the use of ACE inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers (ACEI/ARB) and beta-blockers were collected only at baseline. Therefore, the potential impact of cardioprotective medications introduced during follow-up on imaging findings could not be assessed.
In patients with lymphoma undergoing anthracycline-based chemotherapy, subclinical and progressive cardiac dysfunction is frequent and can be detected by both TTE and CMR, with CMR-derived feature-tracking strain identifying more frequent detection of myocardial functional abnormalities. The consistent rise in hs-cTnT and the progressive deterioration of biventricular function and myocardial deformation reinforce the value of a multiparametric imaging strategy in cardio-oncology surveillance. These findings support the incorporation of CMR into the routine follow-up of high-risk patients, enabling to identify CTRCD and timely cardioprotective intervention.
Competencies in medical knowledge: These findings highlight the presence of subclinical, progressive myocardial dysfunction detectable by both TTE and CMR in patients undergoing potentially cardiotoxic chemotherapy. The consistent alterations in strain and morphofunctional parameters underscore the importance of multiparametric imaging for early detection and longitudinal monitoring of cardiotoxic effects.
Translational outlook: Further large-scale, multicenter, and longer-term studies are needed to establish the prognostic role of CMR-derived myocardial strain in the routine surveillance of anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity and to define optimal thresholds for triggering cardioprotective therapy.

The in vitro generation of human vascular cells (e.g. smooth muscle cells (SMCs), vascular endothelial cells (VECs)) represents a promising approach to regenerate compromised vascular beds (Leeper et al., 2010), as well as to model specific features of vascular dysfunction (e.g. blood brain barrier damage) (Vatine et al., 2019). Among the available strategies, direct reprogramming of skin fibroblasts into functional cells was previously reported for blood progenitor cells (Szabo et al., 2010), SMCs (van Tuyn et al., 2005) and VECs (Han et al., 2014; Morita et al., 2015). Direct reprogramming of cells from skin biopsies offers a critical advantage compared to other approaches such as the differentiation of induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells. Indeed, although iPS cells have significantly contributed to the discovery of novel disease mechanisms (Park et al., 2019) as well as to the pre-clinical screening of promising drug candidates (Zhang et al., 2019), the differentiation process of iPS cells requires a mandatory transit through an embryonic-like state which was reported to reset the aging profile of the cells of origin (Mertens et al., 2015). Conversely, direct reprogramming from skin fibroblasts was shown to maintain the cellular signature of aging and to highlight critical factors of human aging in neurons (Mertens et al., 2015).

Strikingly, it was demonstrated that ETV2 alone, which is a master regulator of VEC development and early vasculogenesis (Qiu and Hirschi, 2019), was sufficient to in vitro reprogram human skin fibroblasts into functional VECs (Morita et al., 2015). Similarly, the induced expression of myocardin (MYOCD) was able to strongly induce both smooth and cardiac muscle genes in human foreskin fibroblasts and mesenchymal stem cells (van Tuyn et al., 2005).

paragraphs.section: Induced vascular cells show gene-expression and functional differences between young vs. old donors
paragraphs.text: In parallel, DE analysis performed on iVECs highlighted the upregulation of GSTM1 and PALD1 in cells derived from old vs. young donors. GSTM1 is generally activated in presence of oxidative stress and inflammatory conditions (Lopes-Aguiar et al., 2017), while PALD1 is an endothelial-specific gene inhibiting endothelial junction stability (Nitzsche, 2016). To test if these genes were actually dysregulated in human donors, we analyzed human skin biopsies and found that CD31+ VECs from old vs. young healthy donors indeed expressed higher levels of PALD1 (194.9 ± 30.0% vs. 100.0±24.3% after normalization, Figure 2D and F; Videos 4 and 5) and GSTM1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). However, the paper does not directly address the connection between GSTM1 and cardiac strain or heart muscle damage caused by Adriamycin. Paragraph 30 establishes that GSTM1 is upregulated in cells derived from older donors compared to younger ones, and this finding is consistent across both human skin biopsies and mouse models. However, the paper does not directly address the connection between GSTM1 and cardiac strain or heart muscle damage caused by Adriamycin.

paragraphs.text: This study investigated the association between genetic variants and the occurrence of oral mucositis (OM) in pediatric patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and lymphoma undergoing chemotherapy (CT). A retrospective observational longitudinal study was conducted, with daily assessment of OM using the World Health Organization scale and blood samples collected for DNA extraction. Genetic variants were analyzed through next-generation sequencing, using a gene panel focused on 67 coding regions within 20 genes. Sixty-four pediatric patients were evaluated during 392 cycles of CT, with the most commonly used protocols being doxorubicin (DOXO) (34.2%), methotrexate (MTX) (27.8%), and cyclophosphamide (CTX) (17.3%). paragraphs.section: Knocking out DIC-related genes alters the hiPSC-CM response to doxorubicin treatment
paragraphs.text: Of the 35 genes studied, 3 gene KOs were protective of DIC (SLC28A3, SLC22A17, and SLC28A1), 6 gene KOs did not have a significant effect on DIC (ATP2B1, HNMT, POR, CYBA, WDR4, and COL1A2), and 26 KOs increased DIC (ABCC10, ABCC2, ABCB4, ABCC5, ABCC9, CAT, CBR1, CBR3, CYP2J2, ERBB2, GPX3, GSTM1, GSTP1, HAS3, HFE, MLH1, MYH7, NOS3, PLCE1, PRDM2, RAC2, RARG, RIN3, SPG7, CELF4, and ZFN521).

paragraphs.section: ROS production is the major mechanism causing DIC
paragraphs.text: The largest functional group studied comprised genes related to ROS production. H2O2 production analysis in cardiomyocytes exposed to doxorubicin revealed reduced production in CBR1-KO and CBR3-KO hiPSC-CMs, indicating a potential link to cardiotoxicity via reduced metabolism of doxorubicin to doxorubicinol by carbonyl reductases. In contrast, HAS3-KO, SPG7-KO, GSTM1-KO, and RAC2-KO exhibited higher ROS production and increased sensitivity to doxorubicin, indicating a role of these genes in H2O2 handling. Notably, no significant differences in H2O2 production were observed in CAT-KO, NOS3-KO, PLCE1-KO, GPX3-KO, ERBB2-KO, and GSTP1-KO. This might suggest that the DIC observed in the KO of these genes is due to the defects in the handling and detoxification of additional ROS products and/or

paragraphs.section: Genes involved in ROS production and handling
paragraphs.text: The largest group of genes in our list (12 of 35) is associated with ROS production and handling (Table 1). We assessed the H2O2 levels in hiPSC-CMs after 24 hours of doxorubicin treatment (Figures 3A to 3C). After doxorubicin treatment, our analysis indicated that ROS levels were lower in CBR1-KO (half maximal inhibitory concentration [IC50] = 20.6 mM; P = 0.0024) and CBR3-KO (IC50 = 31 mM; P = 0.0069) hiPSC-CMs compared with isogenic control hiPSC-CMs (IC50 = 4.1 mM) (Figure 3A). However, after doxorubicin treatment, ROS levels were increased in SPG7-KO (IC50 = 0.3 mM; P = 0.0006), HAS3-KO (IC50 = 0.1 mM; P = 0.0023), GSTM1-KO (IC50 = 0.26 mM; P = 0.039), and RAC2-KO (IC50 = 0.5 mM; P = 0.04) hiPSC-CMs (Figure 3B). No significant differences in ROS production were detected in PLCE1-KO, E

paragraphs.section: Genes involved in doxorubicin uptake and efflux
paragraphs.text: Upon increasing the doxorubicin concentration to 3 μM, all the cells, except for ABCC10-KO, exhibited significant differences in doxorubicin uptake compared with control. Doxorubicin uptake was significantly lower in SLC22A17-KO (43.55% ± 3.04%; P = 0.0005), SLC28A1-KO (35.11% ± 2.63%; P < 0.0001), and SLC28A3-KO (35.24% ± 1.36%; P < 0.0001) hiPSC-CMs compared with isogenic control hiPSC-CMs (57.68% ± 3.11%) (Figure 4A). Conversely, 3-μM doxorubicin treatment led to significantly higher doxorubicin uptake in ABCB4-KO (71.77% ± 3.02%; P = 0.0001), ABCC2-KO (74.52% ± 1.57%; P = 0.0003), ABCC5-KO (79.52% ± 3.79%; P < 0.0001), and ABCC9-KO (68.57% ± 1.02%; P = 0.04) hiPSC-CMs (Figure 4A).

paper_digests.title: Recommendations for genetic testing to reduce the incidence of anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity.

paragraphs.text: Anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity (ACT) occurs in 57% of treated patients and remains an important limitation of anthracycline-based chemotherapy. In various genetic association studies, potential genetic risk markers for ACT have been identified. Therefore, we developed evidence-based clinical practice recommendations for pharmacogenomic testing to further individualize therapy based on ACT risk. We followed a standard guideline development process, including a systematic literature search, evidence synthesis and critical appraisal, and the development of clinical practice recommendations with an international expert group. paragraphs.text: Further assessments of molecular phenotypes linked to mitochondrial injury verified that miR-210-3p regulates doxorubicin-triggered mitochondrial damage. Western blot analysis of myocardial tissues revealed that miR-210-3p overexpression reversed the DOX-induced downregulation of mitochondrial electron transport chain complex proteins (NDUFS1, ATP5A1, SDHB and COX IV), indicating improved molecular signatures associated with mitochondrial respiration (Fig. 7H and I). In addition, miR-210-3p overexpression suppressed DOX-mediated upregulation of ACVR1B and phosphorylation of SMAD3. In this study, ACVR1B was identified as a target gene of miR-210-3p through cross-prediction using four authoritative databases (miRDB, miRTarBase, miRWalk, and starBase). As a member of the transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) superfamily, ACVR1B primarily regulates downstream signaling pathways by mediating the phosphorylation of SMAD family proteins [24, 25]. Aberrant activation of the ACVR1B-SMAD3 signaling pathway is closely associated with the pathogenesis and progression of cardiovascular diseases, such as promoting myocardial fibrosis and exacerbating myocardial remodeling [25–28]. [PMID 40859847] (British journal of clinical pharmacology, 2026) Development of a predictive model for neutropenia risk in Japanese breast cancer patients treated with doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide. Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia (CIN) and febrile neutropenia (FN) are important considerations for anticancer drug dosing. Recent studies suggest that CIN may also improve survival. This study aimed to assess the impact of CIN on survival outcomes in breast cancer patients and to develop a predictive model for CIN incorporating genetic factors. In 166 breast cancer patients treated with doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide (AC therapy), neutropenia was classified into three severity groups using CTCAE v5.0 criteria. The relationship between severe CIN and survival was analysed. Additionally, 33 genetic polymorphisms linked to pharmacokinetics and susceptibility were examined, and a predictive model for CIN was built using multivariate logistic regression integrating clinical and genetic factors. Among patients receiving AC therapy, the 10-year survival rates were 80.6% for the Grades 0-2 group, 96.2% for the Grades 3-4 group without FN, and 79.0% for the Grades 3-4 group with FN, indicating that patients in the Grades 3-4 group without FN had significantly longer survival. A predictive model for Grade 4 CIN was developed using seven factors: age, haemoglobin levels, serum creatinine levels, and the genetic polymorphisms ABCB1 rs1128503, ERCC1 rs11615, ERCC2 rs238406 and XRCC3 rs709399. The model had an AUC of 0.744 (95% CI, 0.666-0.823), and including genetic polymorphisms improved predictive accuracy by 0.128 (P = 0.004). CIN was linked to improved survival in breast cancer patients. The predictive model including genetic factors provided a more accurate assessment of CIN risk, potentially enabling more personalized treatment approaches.
[PMID 33160994] (Life sciences, 2021) Reserpine inhibits DNA repair, cell proliferation, invasion and induces apoptosis in oral carcinogenesis via modulation of TGF-β signaling. Reserpine is a natural indole alkaloid isolated from Rauwolfia serpentina and has potent antioxidant, antimicrobial, and anti-mutagenic properties. Accordingly, this study aimed to investigate the effect of reserpine on DNA repair, cell proliferation, invasion and apoptosis in 7,12-dimethylbenz[a]anthracene(DMBA)-induced hamster buccal pouch (HBP) carcinogenesis. Transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) was found to induce Smad2, 3 and 4 phosphorylation triggering Smad3/Snail mediated DNA repair proteins and Smad2/4 nuclear translocation. In contrast, reserpine inhibits TGF-β dependent Smad2/3/4 phosphorylation, thereby blockage Smad3/Snail activation and Smad2/4 nuclear translocation. Interruption of these oncogenic signaling pathways leads to downregulating ERCC1, XPF, Ku70, DNA-PKcs, PCNA, cyclin D1, HIF-1α, IL-6, Mcl-1 and stimulates Bax, cytochrome C, Apaf-1, caspase-9, caspase-3 and PARP protein expressions. This study provides therapeutic potential of reserpine in inhibiting DNA repair, cell proliferation, and invasion while simultaneously inducing apoptosis via modulation TGF-β signals.

paragraphs.text: We previously detailed a quantitative systems toxicology modeling framework for early prediction of chemotherapeutic-induced clinical intestinal adverse effects. The model describes stem and progenitor cell dynamics in the small intestinal epithelium and integrates epithelial-related processes, such as transcriptional profiles, citrulline kinetics, and the probability that the organism will have diarrhea. This protocol describes a step-by-step guide to the examples detailed in the original manuscript, namely 5-FU- and doxorubicin-induced intestinal toxicity.

paper_digests.summary: The paper discusses a modeling framework for predicting chemotherapeutic-induced intestinal adverse effects, including mucositis-like symptoms. However, it does not provide specific information on whether doxorubicin causes genetic predisposition to mucositis.
